claims.text: The target material is bulk, as-cast HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
A machine-learning model would be trained on measured thermal-conductivity data from similar alloys and specimens with known defect and impurity concentrations.
The proposed model applies across the nearly 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The proposed model applies to bulk polycrystalline HfNbTaTiZr samples containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Machine learning trained on experimental data will predict HfNbTaTiZr thermal conductivity more accurately than traditional analytical models such as Debye or Callaway models.
Traditional analytical models assume perfect, defect-free crystals.
The machine-learning model can learn the effects of oxygen impurities and other defects directly from experimental data.
Oxygen impurities and other defects affect phonon scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
The defect-induced change in phonon scattering affects thermal conductivity.
Analytical models neglect defect and impurity effects because they assume perfect crystals.
The machine-learning predictions will be within 10% of measured thermal conductivity across both specified temperature regimes.
Analytical-model predictions may deviate from measurements by 20–50% because they neglect defects and impurities.
Defect-free analytical predictions typically overestimate the conductivity of real, impure HfNbTaTiZr samples.
Applicability is limited to bulk polycrystalline HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen concentrations no greater than 1 wt.%.
Accuracy may degrade for single crystals, oxygen concentrations above 1 wt.%, or temperatures outside 0–1200 K.
Prediction accuracy depends on having sufficient and representative training data covering the relevant defect and impurity regimes.
Deviations greater than 20%, or performance not significantly better than the analytical models, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The prediction requires error within 10%, but the absolute-error falsification threshold is greater than 20%. Results between 10% and 20% would violate the quantitative prediction without falsifying it under that rule.

Applicability is stated for two disjoint ranges, 0–200 K and 300–1200 K, while degradation is described only outside 0–1200 K, leaving the unclaimed 200–300 K interval ambiguously inside the overall boundary.
